thread.title: General Motors Stock Is Plunging. Blame Apple.

title: General Motors Stock Is Plunging. Blame Apple.
text:
General Motors Stock Is Plunging. Blame Apple. By Jan. 3, 2019 12:00 p.m. ET Order Reprints Vehicles at GM’s Cadillac House in New York. Photograph by Spencer Platt/Getty Images Text size
General Motors (GM), along with several other auto makers, reported its 2018 car sales this morning. Its U.S. deliveries dropped 2.7% in the fourth quarter and fell 1.6% for the full year, to just under 3 million units.
That has GM shares down by 2.6% in Thursday morning trading, to $32.77. Yet the price decline probably isn’t a result of disappointing sales. In fact, the seasonally adjusted annualized selling rate (the “automotive SAAR”) for North American light vehicles is expected to be over 17 million units in December—and 2018 will be the fourth straight year U.S. light vehicle sales topped 17 million units. Elon Musk unveiled the first mile-long tunnel in Hawthorne, Calif., on Tuesday. The tech entrepreneur says the system, simply called “loop,” is a first step toward developing a high-speed network underground to eliminate traffic congestion. Photo: Pool/Getty Images
Instead of deliveries, it’s far more likely that GM’s plunge is due to Apple ’s (AAPL) guidance cut, which has stoked additional fears about the Chinese consumer economy. Apple cut its quarterly revenue guidance from $91 billion to $84 billion Wednesday evening, setting off another round of selling in Apple and Apple supplier shares.
Don’t forget that China is the largest car market in the world, and Chinese exposure to U.S. automotive companies tends to be higher than Chinese exposure to other manufacturing sectors. For auto and auto-parts companies, exposure ranges from about 10% to 20% of sales, about double the exposure compared with other U.S.-based industrial companies.
Even before Apple’s announcement, sales in the Middle Kingdom were decelerating. Baird analyst David Leiker recently wrote that “Chinese auto sales declined 14% year over year in November. Auto production declined 19% year over year in November.” He added, “this is well below what [we] believe is recent fourth quarter consensus.”
Even so, after a year when GM stock fell 18% and the Russell 3000 Auto & Auto Parts index fell 23%, it’s worth asking if there is an opportunity in depressed automotive shares. GM stock now trades for under five times next year’s estimated earnings, down from about seven times earnings a year ago.
There is some good news for GM in today’s announcement. The company noted that it is “very bullish on pickups heading into 2019.” Chevy will launch its next-generation Silverado in the second half of 2019. Trucks tend to be the highest-value products in domestic auto maker’s lineups.
For 2019, Williams Research Partners analyst Michael Ward argues that another 17 million light vehicles will be sold in North America. He also points out that the “tech and auto worlds have been converging and 2019 could be the biggest year thus far.” After all, ride-sharing companies Lyft and Uber Technologies are expected to offer shares to the public later this year. Newsletter Sign-up
GM, along with several other car companies, will update investors in a couple of weeks at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit. Based on the Chinese slowdown, auto guidance may underwhelm the Street. Still, investor sentiment should improve if the U.S. and China can agree on trade, if the Federal Reserve stops raising rates, and if some of the Chinese stimulus can spur credit growth in the second half of 2019.
Those are three big ifs, to be sure. But if the macro environment improves, investors can stop worrying and start thinking about some of the positive technological trends reshaping the industry.
